ink Drug Hub. Launched in March 2022, any professional from across the county can access resources, including free drug and alcohol awareness training. The training is evidence-based and developed in collaboration with partner agencies and experts.

There are currently 8 modules, including one on having conversations with children and young people about drugs, launched in July 2025. Bespoke courses are also available on request.

Over 1,300 people have been trained, with a strong uptake from:

children’s social workers

mental health workers

youth workers

early help practitioners

housing officers

foster carers

parents and carers

Over 250 people have completed the children and young people’s module. The training has been provided to trainee social workers and to newly qualified social workers one year into practice. Around two-thirds of these trainees intend to move into children’s social work practice.

The latest session was run in collaboration with the local lived experience recovery organisation (LERO). This brought the voices of people with lived experience into the session, including people who began taking substances as young people, as well as current parents and carers. These sessions will run annually with each new intake of social workers.

Drink Drug Hub forms part of North Yorkshire’s strategic ambition to ensure consistent training and non-stigmatised practice across the county’s workforce.

6. Safeguarding

Promoting and safeguarding child welfare

Promoting and safeguarding child welfare refers to:

preventing harm to children’s health or development

providing timely interventions to prevent problems escalating

protecting children from exploitation, abuse and neglect

Alcohol and drug services working with children have a critical role to play in promoting and safeguarding child welfare.

It is also important to note that some vulnerable young people aged 18 to 24, such as care leavers or those on an education, health and care (EHC) plan, may still receive social care support. For more information on EHC plans, see Children with special educational needs and disabilities.

What services should do about safeguarding

Children and young people’s alcohol and drug services should:

have internal policies and procedures on emerging risk and safeguarding, in line with local reporting and protocols, and agreed with Families First and local safeguarding children partnerships

immediately refer to children’s social care any child who is dependent on alcohol or drugs

ensure all staff are trained in child and adult safeguarding and know how to work in line with safeguarding procedures, including reporting and taking part in multi-agency safeguarding assessments and covering areas such as child sexual and criminal exploitation, violence and abuse

understand their role and obligations as set out in Working together to safeguard children, the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 and the Care Act 2014 factsheets, as well as operational guidance such as in the ‘Families First Partnership programme’

have a nominated safeguarding lead responsible for welfare of children and young people and ensuring appropriate and timely information sharing with local partners, such as multi-agency safeguarding hubs, CAMHS, schools and youth offending teams

have a safeguarding lead responsible for reviewing quality governance arrangements for children and young people’s services

A multi-agency and co-located model for services in East Sussex: case study

East Sussex has a well-established, multi-agency substance misuse service for young people aged 25 and under delivered by children’s services. The team is made up of a range of professionals. These include social workers, nurses and CAMHS workers, alongside children and young people’s drug and alcohol workers.

Staff work within an integrated management protocol and to a detailed service specification, which outlines delivery to identified vulnerable groups. Many staff are co-located in services, for example youth justice, care leavers and the child criminal exploitation team. The service also provides specific screening and service access pathways for children who have been excluded from school and those accessing emergency departments.

Any worker with sufficient alcohol and drugs training may act as lead professional, regardless of their specialism.

For all children 17 and under and care leavers up to the age of 25, co-located workers use a shared case record system. This allows alcohol and drug assessment and interventions to be included seamlessly within statutory planning processes.

The engagement and retention of children and young people in treatment is high in East Sussex, as is the children’s workforce confidence in working with alcohol and drug use issues. The multi-agency and co-located model is a significant factor in the service’s effectiveness.

7. Multi-agency complex care arrangements

Community-based treatment

Community-based treatments are usually more appropriate and effective for children and young people than interventions that temporarily remove them from their family and support network.

Differences in emotional and cognitive development, problem awareness and readiness for change, as well as consent and safeguarding issues, all require a different approach. This means that residential rehabilitation designed for adults does not easily translate to children’s services. Professionals working with children and young people should always consider local solutions before looking for residential placements.

Complex care

Complex care comprises intensive, multi-agency care packages for extremely vulnerable children and young people. A child or young person may need complex care when they:

are experiencing significant harm, and need substantial additional support, related to their alcohol or drug use

Local areas may decide that a full needs assessment is not needed every year. But as a minimum, every year commissioners should:

engage children and young people with lived and living experience to inform local commissioning and service delivery

update alcohol and drug treatment data to inform local planning

review other local data sources, intelligence and service performance

Needs assessments should inform and be guided by part of the local council’s wider strategic needs assessment for children and young people. They should be jointly owned by relevant local partners, including:

CAMHS

early help

children’s social care

multi-agency child protection teams

youth offending teams

Service plans

Service plans should be based on needs assessments, involving relevant commissioning and delivery partners. These include:

members of the local combating drugs partnership (see section 3)

the service’s nominated child protection lead (for a definition, see the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) resource Nominated child protection lead or designated safeguarding officer)

children and young people with lived or living experience

parents or carers of children accessing alcohol and drug services

Identifying local assets

As well as identifying gaps in provision, commissioners should identify local assets. These are assets that are already supporting or could potentially support the health and wellbeing of children and young people. This includes those with, or at risk of developing, alcohol or drug problems.

‘Asset-based community development’ is a commissioning approach that uses community (and individual) strengths and resources, or assets, as the foundation for improving public health. It involves bringing together local associations, services, groups, networks and residents to identify, access and strengthen local assets that promote health and wellbeing.

In Bolton, the adult and children and young people’s drug and alcohol services were co-designed with local people with lived experience, alongside other local partners. This community-centred approach became part of the commissioning processes, to ensure that services reflected local needs, assets, priorities and insights. The services have continued to work closely with a network of trusted local organisations and stakeholders, providing individuals and families with accessible and familiar routes to advice, support and treatment. This approach aligns with the principles of community-based support and integrated family services in Best Start Family Hubs and Healthy Babies: guidance for local authorities.

In Northumberland, services have adopted an asset-based approach that builds on rural community networks. They use outreach in rural communities and peer workers to help people who are not in treatment access support. This helps connect isolated residents with harm-reduction support and mainstream healthcare.

Having identified local assets, commissioners should support children and young people to access them. Where appropriate and safe to do so, they should also support the development of those assets, following an assessment of safeguarding and other potential risks.

Improving access to specialist interventions in London: case study

The London region of the Association of Directors of Public Health (ADPH), in partnership with the Department of Health and Social Care’s national and London regional teams, hosted a London regional practice improvement event on 11 July 2024. The event brought together 98 professionals working with children and young people in relation to alcohol and drug use across the capital, including public health leads, commissioners and providers.

The event focused on what could be done to improve children and young people’s access to specialist alcohol and drug interventions in London. There were presentations on research, London data and local case studies, each informing improvements to service effectiveness. Delegates were invited to suggest themes to be considered in future national, regional and local policy.

Several themes emerged as priorities, including the need for:

more intensive support for complex cases

better data recording and sharing among services

services to be welcoming, non-stigmatising and designed with input from children and young people

The ADPH region then developed a Practice improvement self-assessment checklist. The checklist helps areas to have discussions about current provision, and identify barriers, opportunities and actions to improve services. Commissioners of children and young people’s drug and alcohol treatment services should complete this checklist with their service providers, and in consultation with:

children’s social care

education providers

youth justice

other relevant sectors, including mental health and family services

For more information, see Improving access to drug and alcohol services for young Londoners.

2. Interventions and delivery models

Local councils should commission evidence-based universal and targeted interventions for children and young people in a variety of settings, while also making a range of specialist interventions available.

For clinical guidelines on specialist interventions, see ‘Clinical guidelines for alcohol treatment’ and ‘Drug misuse and dependence: UK guidelines on clinical management’.

Universal prevention

Universal prevention interventions are for all children and young people.

Information and education

Different services, such as youth offending teams, CAMHS and statutory children’s services, transition young people at different ages or developmental stages. These different arrangements should be detailed in the transitional care plan, so that everyone knows which agencies are involved, what support they are providing and when it is due to end.

Young people with care experience and those with EHC plans have legal entitlements to receive support for education, health, housing and life skills up to age 25. This can include remaining in a children and young people’s alcohol and drug service.

Children and young people’s alcohol and drug services are responsible for making sure that young people in their care are prepared for the transition to an adult alcohol and drug service. Where it is safe and appropriate, parents or carers should also be prepared for the transition.

Both children and young people’s and adult alcohol and drug services are responsible for making sure young adults receive continuous support. As a minimum, each service and the young person should review and update the final care plan before transition. Where possible, parents or carers should be involved in transition planning.

Supporting young people not in education, employment or training

Children and young people who are NEET, or who are at risk of becoming NEET, should receive co-ordinated support.

As part of their assessment and care planning, services should understand a young person’s education, employment and training status and any barriers to participating in them.

Where appropriate, services should establish pathways to education, employment and skills support, including individual placement and support (IPS) services. IPS is an evidence-based approach that helps people find and stay in work alongside treatment and recovery support.

A recent report on the outcomes of IPS found that 62% of people aged 24 and under who accessed IPS moved into employment, and around three-quarters of those who found work stayed in it for more than 13 weeks.

As well as supporting people into work, IPS can help young people start or return to education, training and apprenticeships. Participating in education, training and employment can support recovery and a successful transition to adulthood.

Employment support in South Tyneside and Gateshead: case study

Emerging adults aged 16 to 24 with alcohol or drug problems can face unique challenges when entering employment. These include:

uncertainty about career goals

balancing education and work

managing personal barriers, such as trauma, neurodiversity and mental health problems

South Tyneside and Gateshead councils have a dedicated IPS employment specialist for young people aged 16 and over. This ensures individually tailored support that enables young people to thrive in the workplace.

The employment specialist sits within the young person’s treatment team and works closely with recovery workers. They also work with a range of other partners as required, including:

social care and safeguarding teams

the young person’s education provider

training and apprenticeship providers

the young person’s family

The standard IPS model is adapted to recognise that young people:

often need more time and flexibility

may simultaneously need support to stay in or return to education

may want to explore work opportunities that include educational elements

may benefit from family involvement, where appropriate

This approach allows the employment specialist to support young people into sustainable employment by addressing their specific challenges.

Increasing engagement with alcohol and drug treatment services in Derbyshire: case study

Derbyshire County Council has developed a dedicated service for emerging adults called 1625 Outreach, delivered by Change Grow Live. It is a multi-component, community-based model designed to increase access and engagement from 16 to 25 year olds who would not typically use alcohol and drug treatment services.

The service relies heavily on integrated partnership working to operate from a range of age-appropriate, place-based settings, including:

night-time economy venues, such as pubs and bars

festivals and other large, organised events

further and higher education settings

community hotspots like youth centres

The service provides targeted, responsive support through a range of innovative engagement methods, including pop-up stalls, education workshops and a mobile unit. Digital outreach is also an important feature, using a range of social media platforms to promote age-appropriate harm reduction content.

These targeted, early interventions aim to reduce illicit substance use and related risk-taking behaviours among 16 to 24 year olds that are at increased risk of experiencing alcohol or drug-related harm. The service also acts as an accessible first point of contact for those who may need more structured treatment, with direct referral pathways into both young people’s and adult alcohol and drug services in Derbyshire.

In 2025, the service engaged 6,312 young people aged 16 to 24 across these place-based settings. Of these:

44% had used cocaine

43% had used ketamine

36% had used nitrous oxide

A total of 76 referrals were made into treatment services for continued, care-planned interventions.

A feasibility study to evaluate the 1625 Outreach service has been published on the ‘Our research’ page of the Change Grow Live website. Aspects of the model have since been adopted in Sheffield, Derby, Nottingham and Liverpool.
